items.snippet_en: AP News reported on April 2, 2020, that the claim of hot water with lemon and bicarbonate of soda curing coronavirus is false. This drink is not a cure, and no herbal remedies are recommended for COVID-19.

National Academies stated on April 22, 2020, that consuming acidic drinks like lemon juice has no effect on coronavirus infections. Lemon juice will not destroy viruses or stop the virus-copying process, and drinking it hot will not prevent or cure COVID-19.

The Guardian reported on March 26, 2020, about "dangerous quack cures" for coronavirus, including lemon juice and hot water, being shared online. The government advised reporting such content to social media companies.

Times of Israel debunked on April 5, 2020, the false claim that Israel avoided coronavirus deaths by prescribing hot water, lemon, and bicarbonate of soda. Experts confirm there is no proof this or any herbal remedy protects against COVID-19.

CBS News reported on May 5, 2020, that consuming acidic liquids like lemon juice will not kill the coronavirus. Dr. Mallika Marshall emphasized that social distancing, good handwashing, and self-care are the best protections.

FactCheck.org debunked on April 2, 2020, a social media post falsely claiming a blend of sodium bicarbonate and lemon juice would "eliminate" the novel coronavirus and prevented COVID-19 deaths in Israel. The claim is baseless.

outputs.notes_en: All sources contradict the claim that drinking hot water mixed with lemon juice will destroy the coronavirus. Multiple sources specifically address and debunk this claim, often in conjunction with bicarbonate of soda, stating it is false and not a cure or preventative measure for COVID-19.
